title: The OSI Model & What's on the Network

sections.title: The OSI Model — 7 Layers
sections.content:
The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model is a 7-layer framework for how data moves across a network. It is conceptual — real stacks (TCP/IP) collapse some layers — but the exam uses it to locate problems and describe where devices and protocols operate.
Layer | Name | Job | Data unit
7 | Application | Interface to the user's apps (HTTP, DNS, SMTP) | Data
6 | Presentation | Formatting, encryption, compression (TLS, ASCII, JPEG) | Data
5 | Session | Starts/maintains/ends conversations between hosts | Data
4 | Transport | End-to-end delivery, segmentation, TCP/UDP, port numbers | Segment
3 | Network | Logical addressing + routing between networks (IP) | Packet
2 | Data Link | Framing + MAC addressing on the local link (switches) | Frame
1 | Physical | Bits on the wire — cables, connectors, voltages, radio | Bits
Mnemonic (7 to 1): All People Seem To Need Data Processing.
Encapsulation: as data moves DOWN the stack on the sender, each layer wraps it with its own header (and L2 adds a trailer). On the receiver it moves UP, and each layer strips its header. A unit named by the layer below it is 'encapsulated' inside that frame/packet/segment.
exam_tips: Know the data unit per layer: segment (L4), packet (L3), frame (L2), bits (L1).
A switch is Layer 2 (MAC); a router is Layer 3 (IP). A 'Layer 3 switch' does both.
Port numbers live at Layer 4; IP addresses at Layer 3; MAC addresses at Layer 2.

sections.title: Where Devices & Protocols Live
sections.content:
Mapping appliances to OSI layers is a favorite exam move.
Layer 1 (Physical): hubs, repeaters, media converters, cables, transceivers (SFP), patch panels. A hub repeats bits to every port — one big collision domain.
Layer 2 (Data Link): switches and bridges forward frames by MAC address. Each switch port is its own collision domain; a VLAN or the switch defines a broadcast domain. NICs operate here (and L1).
Layer 3 (Network): routers forward packets between networks by IP and separate broadcast domains. Layer 3 switches route between VLANs.
Layer 4-7: firewalls (L3/L4 stateful, up to L7 next-gen), load balancers (L4 or L7), proxies (L7), IDS/IPS, and WAFs (L7).
Collision domain vs broadcast domain: a switch BREAKS UP collision domains (one per port) but forwards broadcasts, so all switch ports share one broadcast domain. A router BREAKS UP broadcast domains.
exam_tips: Switch = more collision domains, same broadcast domain. Router = separate broadcast domains.
Next-gen firewalls (NGFW) and WAFs inspect up to Layer 7 (application content).

sections.title: Networking Appliances & Functions
sections.content:
Common boxes and what they do:
Router — connects different networks, forwards by IP, runs routing protocols, often does NAT at the edge.
Switch — connects hosts on the same network, forwards by MAC, supports VLANs, trunking, PoE.
Firewall — permits/denies traffic by rules; stateful firewalls track connection state. NGFW adds app awareness, IDS/IPS, and user identity.
Load balancer — distributes client requests across a server pool for scale and availability (round-robin, least-connections).
Proxy — forward proxy sits in front of clients (caching, filtering, anonymity); reverse proxy sits in front of servers (offload, security).
IDS/IPS — Intrusion Detection (alerts, out-of-band) vs Intrusion Prevention (blocks, in-line).
VPN concentrator / headend — terminates many VPN tunnels.
Wireless controller (WLC) — centrally manages many access points.
NAS/SAN — network-attached storage (file-level, over the LAN) vs storage area network (block-level, dedicated fabric like Fibre Channel/iSCSI).
Content delivery network (CDN) — geographically distributed caches that serve content close to users.
exam_tips: IDS detects and alerts (passive); IPS sits in-line and can drop traffic (active).
Forward proxy protects/represents clients; reverse proxy protects/represents servers.
NAS = file-level over existing LAN; SAN = block-level over a dedicated high-speed fabric.

sections.title: TCP/IP Model vs OSI
sections.content:
The TCP/IP (DoD) model is the one the internet actually runs on, with 4 layers that map onto OSI:
TCP/IP layer | OSI layers it covers
Application | 7, 6, 5 (Application, Presentation, Session)
Transport | 4 (Transport) — TCP and UDP
Internet | 3 (Network) — IP, ICMP, routing
Link / Network Access | 2, 1 (Data Link, Physical)
So HTTP/DNS/TLS all sit in TCP/IP 'Application', while OSI splits them across L5-L7. The exam may ask you to translate between the two models.
exam_tips: TCP/IP Application layer = OSI layers 5, 6, and 7 combined.
Both models share the Transport (L4) and Network/Internet (L3) layers one-to-one.

concept_cards.hook: Wrapping data with each layer's header as it moves down the OSI stack (and stripping them on the way up); the reverse is de-encapsulation.
A network segment where devices share bandwidth and frames can collide. A switch gives each port its own collision domain.
The set of devices that receive one another's broadcast frames. A router (or a VLAN boundary) separates broadcast domains.
A firewall that tracks the state of active connections and allows return traffic for sessions it has already permitted.
A proxy placed in front of servers that receives client requests on their behalf — used for SSL offload, caching, and security.
Intrusion Detection System alerts on suspicious traffic (passive, out-of-band); Intrusion Prevention System sits in-line and can block it (active).
Storage Area Network — provides block-level storage over a dedicated high-speed fabric (Fibre Channel or iSCSI), appearing to servers as local disks.
A switch that also routes between VLANs/subnets at wire speed, combining Layer 2 switching with Layer 3 IP forwarding.

practice_questions.q: Which OSI layer is responsible for logical addressing and path selection between networks?
practice_questions.explanation: The Network layer handles logical (IP) addressing and routing between networks.

practice_questions.q: Which device forwards frames based only on MAC addresses?
practice_questions.explanation: A switch builds a MAC table and forwards frames by destination MAC at Layer 2.

practice_questions.q: At which OSI layer do hubs and repeaters operate?
practice_questions.explanation: Hubs and repeaters just regenerate electrical signals/bits, which is Layer 1 work.

practice_questions.q: A forward proxy primarily represents and protects whom?
practice_questions.explanation: A forward proxy sits in front of clients, handling caching, filtering, and anonymity for outbound traffic.

practice_questions.q: Which protocol data unit (PDU) is used at the Data Link layer?
practice_questions.explanation: Layer 2 uses frames; Layer 3 packets, Layer 4 segments, Layer 1 bits.

practice_questions.q: Which appliance caches and distributes content geographically close to users?
practice_questions.explanation: A CDN places cached copies near users to reduce latency and origin load.

practice_questions.q: Which OSI layer establishes, manages, and terminates sessions between applications?
practice_questions.explanation: The Session layer sets up, maintains, and tears down dialogues between hosts.

practice_questions.q: Which provides file-level storage over the existing LAN?
practice_questions.explanation: A NAS serves files over the LAN; a SAN provides block-level storage over a dedicated fabric.

practice_questions.q: MAC addresses are used at which OSI layer?
practice_questions.explanation: MAC (hardware) addressing is a Layer 2 Data Link function.

practice_questions.q: Which device terminates many simultaneous VPN tunnels for remote users?
practice_questions.explanation: A VPN concentrator (headend) terminates and manages large numbers of VPN connections.
